title: The Aragonese riders finish the job. Seven weeks after Ejea, 897 horsemen of the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon run down what is left of the Castilian host at Peñafiel on the Duero, in the heart of Old Castile: 10,886 broken men, of whom 10,564 are cut down or scattered, without the loss of a single Aragonese

title: The stand of the Portuguese, and their fall. With Castile's armies gone, Portugal makes its stand at Portalegre on the Alentejo border, 14,900 against the Emperor's 14,600 with the Aragonese and the Mamlūks beside him. For eighteen days it holds; then it breaks, 7,090 of theirs lost for 3,740 of ours. The war score reaches a hundred

title: The Peace of Ramaḍān with Castile and Portugal, which ends the War of the League and the third war of the Istirdād. Four days after Portalegre, with the war score at a hundred, King Pedro of Castile surrenders, and King Jerónimo of Portugal must follow him. Castile gives up 51 towns, from Salamanca, Ávila and Ciudad Rodrigo in the west through Madrid, Alcalá and Guadalajara to Cuenca, Molina and Requena in the east, with the Cáceres and Plasencia country of upper Extremadura; Portugal gives up 20, Lisbon, Setúbal, Santarém and Évora among them, all the land south of the Tagus mouth and the Alentejo. Castile pays reparations for ten years. All 71 towns pass directly to the crown; the realm grows from 118 towns to 189 and from 1,291,000 people to 2,334,000

title: Fifteen years of building. In the 118 towns the crown held from December 1379 to the eve of the Peace of Ramaḍān, its buildings grew from 598 levels to 698: lumber mills from 9 to 22, eight new bog-iron smelters on the coast of Walba with eight charcoal burners to feed them, banking offices from 1 to 8, jewellers' guilds from 7 to 15, nine more marketplaces and three market warehouses at Ishbīliya, eleven hammams, cotton fields at Sharīsh, Baṭalyaws and Mursiyya, and two slave markets at Ishbīliya. The fleet grew from 4 ships to 16

title: The fourth and last office of the bureaucracy for now: the Dīwān al-Inshāʾ, the chancery that drafts the state's edicts, treaties and letters to foreign courts in the high style of the court. While the crown pays for it, its letters win friends abroad and the realm's subjects are drawn closer; left unpaid, it fumbles its correspondence and the ṭāʾifas resent it

data.precedent: a well-staffed chancery wins friends through eloquent and timely letters, while a neglected one fumbles its correspondence and the realm's standing among other courts suffers for it (the game's text)

title: The diplomatic corps of al-Andalus now reaches across Europe: Paris, Naples, Istanbul and London all receive its ambassadors from time to time. France, unlike Castile, shows itself willing to be a friend, and there is talk at court of an alliance with the French, though it would drag the empire into France's losing war with the English

title: Two new ṭāʾifas are carved from the Castilian lands won at the Peace of Ramaḍān and given to two cousins of the Emperor, sons of his late uncles. Saʿd ibn Ismāʿīl takes the Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka, 21 towns of the Leonese west; Saʿd ibn Faraj, husband of the Emperor's daughter Umm al-Fatḥ, takes the Ṭāʾifa of Qūnka, 20 towns of the Castilian east. Majrīṭ, Cáceres and all the Portuguese lands stay with the crown

title: The court finds al-Ushbūna easier to hold than it feared. With the seas along the Iberian coast growing safer, the city can be reached and governed from the water, and the crown's control there is already far above that of the inland conquests. It is still limited, but in time, with integration, the court expects to bind it to the crown as closely as Qurṭuba
